answer: Physical Layer: Defines electrical, mechanical, and procedural specifications for activating, maintaining, and deactivating the physical link between network devices.
Data Link Layer: Provides node-to-node data transfer and handles error detection from the physical layer. Defines MAC addresses and framing.
Network Layer: Handles routing, logical addressing (IP), and path determination. Responsible for packet forwarding including routing through intermediate routers.
Transport Layer: Provides end-to-end communication, flow control, error correction, and segmentation. Protocols: TCP (connection-oriented) and UDP (connectionless).
Session Layer: Establishes, manages, and terminates sessions between applications. Controls dialog (full-duplex, half-duplex, simplex).
Presentation Layer: Translates data between the application layer and the network format. Handles encryption, compression, and data format conversion (JPEG, ASCII, MPEG).
Application Layer: Provides network services directly to end-user applications. Protocols: HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS, SNMP, SSH, Telnet.

TCP is connection-oriented, reliable, uses 3-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), provides flow control and error correction. UDP is connectionless, faster, no guaranteed delivery, used for streaming and DNS.

1. Client sends SYN
2. Server responds SYN-ACK
3. Client sends ACK
Connection established after ACK is received.
21/FTP, 22/SSH, 23/Telnet, 25/SMTP, 53/DNS, 67/68/DHCP, 80/HTTP, 110/POP3, 143/IMAP, 443/HTTPS, 3389/RDP, 3306/MySQL, 5432/PostgreSQL, 636/LDAPS
20/FTP-data, 21/FTP-control, 22/SSH, 23/Telnet, 25/SMTP, 53/DNS, 80/HTTP, 110/POP3, 143/IMAP, 443/HTTPS, 3389/RDP
53/DNS, 67/DHCP Server, 68/DHCP Client, 69/TFTP, 123/NTP, 161/SNMP, 162/SNMP Trap, 500/ISAKMP/IKE, 514/Syslog, 1900/SSDP

Class A: First octet 1-126 (10.0.0.0/8 private)
Class B: First octet 128-191 (172.16.0.0/12 private)
Class C: First octet 192-223 (192.168.0.0/16 private)
Class D: 224-239 (Multicast)
Class E: 240-255 (Reserved/Research)
48-bit (6 bytes) hardware address, written as 12 hex digits (e.g., 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E). First 24 bits are the OUI (manufacturer), last 24 bits are the device-specific identifier.
255.255.255.255 (limited broadcast) or network-directed broadcast (e.g., 192.168.1.255 for a /24 network). Used by DHCP discover and ARP requests.
Address Resolution Protocol maps IP addresses to MAC addresses. ARP Request is broadcast, ARP Reply is unicast. Gratuitous ARP announces an IP-to-MAC mapping.
Translates private IP addresses to public IP addresses. PAT (Port Address Translation) / NAPT uses port numbers to allow multiple private IPs to share one public IP. Saves IPv4 addresses.
VLSM (Variable Length Subnet Mask) allows subnets of different sizes within the same network. CIDR allows route aggregation. Formula: usable hosts = 2^h - 2 where h = host bits.
Twisted Pair (UTP/STP): Cat5e/Cat6/Cat6a/Cat7/Cat8. Coaxial: RG-58, RG-59, RG-6. Fiber: Single-mode (SMF) and Multi-mode (MMF). Wireless: Radio, Microwave, Infrared, Bluetooth.

Star: All devices connect to a central hub/switch. Bus: All devices on a single cable. Ring: Data travels in one direction. Mesh: Every device connects to every other device (full/partial). Hybrid: Combination of topologies.
n(n-1)/2 connections for n devices. Highly redundant, expensive, difficult to implement. Best for WAN backbone connections and critical infrastructure.
Layer 1: Bits, Layer 2: Frames, Layer 3: Packets, Layer 4: Segments (TCP) / Datagrams (UDP), Layer 5-7: Data
Process of wrapping data with protocol headers at each OSI layer. Application Data → Segment (L4) → Packet (L3) → Frame (L2) → Bits (L1) for transmission.
10BASE-T (10 Mbps, Cat3), 100BASE-TX (Fast Ethernet, 100 Mbps, Cat5), 1000BASE-T (Gigabit, 1 Gbps, Cat5e), 10GBASE-T (10 Gbps, Cat6a), 25G/40G/100G (Fiber/Cat8)
Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection. Used in traditional Ethernet (half-duplex). Devices listen before transmitting, detect collisions, wait random backoff time, then retry.
Half-duplex: Data flows one direction at a time (uses CSMA/CD). Full-duplex: Simultaneous bidirectional communication (no collisions, uses switch dedicated ports).

IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): Virtual machines, storage, networking (AWS EC2, Azure VMs). PaaS (Platform as a Service): Development platforms (Heroku, Google App Engine). SaaS (Software as a Service): Ready-to-use applications (Office 365, Gmail).
Public: Shared infrastructure, multi-tenant. Private: Dedicated to one organization. Hybrid: Combines public and private. Community: Shared by several organizations.
Type 1 (Bare-metal): Hypervisor runs directly on hardware (VMware ESXi, Xen, Hyper-V). Type 2 (Hosted): Hypervisor runs on host OS (VMware Workstation, VirtualBox).
Containers share the host OS kernel (lighter, faster, portable). VMs have full guest OS with virtualized hardware (heavier, isolated). Docker and Kubernetes for container orchestration.
Separates control plane from data plane. Centralized controller manages network traffic. SD-WAN extends SDN across WAN. Provides programmability, flexibility, and centralized management.
Virtual Extensible LAN. Encapsulates Layer 2 frames within UDP packets (typically port 4789). Supports up to 16 million virtual networks (vs 4096 in VLANs). Used for large-scale cloud deployments.
Domain Name System translates domain names to IP addresses. Records: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), NS (nameserver), PTR (reverse), TXT (text/SPF), SOA (authority).
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol. DORA process: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge. Assigns IP, subnet mask, gateway, DNS. Lease time determines how long IP is valid.
128-bit address (8 groups of 4 hex digits). Types: Unicast, Multicast, Anycast, Link-local (fe80::/10). Stateless autoconfiguration (SLAAC) uses Router Advertisements.
Multiple servers share one IP address. Traffic routes to the nearest server. Used for CDN, DNS root servers, load distribution.
One-to-many communication. Packets sent to a multicast group address (224.0.0.0/4). Used for video streaming, IPTV, routing protocols (OSPF, EIGRP).
One-to-all communication on a local network. Limited to the local subnet (routers don't forward broadcasts). Used by ARP, DHCP Discover, NBNS.
Connects a device to a network. Has a MAC address. Supports specific speeds (1 Gbps, 10 Gbps). Can be physical (Ethernet) or wireless (Wi-Fi NIC). VNIC is a software NIC in a VM.
Delivers electrical power over Ethernet cables. Standards: 802.3af (Type 1, 15.4W), 802.3at (Type 2, 30W), 802.3bt (Type 3/4, 60W/90W). Used for IP cameras, VoIP phones, APs.
WLAN: Wireless Local Area Network using Wi-Fi (802.11 standards). WLC: Centralized controller managing multiple access points. Uses CAPWAP protocol for AP management.
802.11b/g/n/ac/ax/be. 802.11n (Wi-Fi 4): 600 Mbps, 2.4/5 GHz. 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5): 6.9 Gbps, 5 GHz. 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6): 9.6 Gbps, 2.4/5 GHz. 802.11be (Wi-Fi 7): 46 Gbps.
SSID: Service Set Identifier - the network name broadcast by an AP. BSSID: Basic Service Set Identifier - the MAC address of the AP. Hidden SSID does not broadcast its name.

WPA: TKIP encryption (deprecated). WPA2: AES-CCMP encryption. WPA3: SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) - protects against offline dictionary attacks. WPA3-Enterprise adds 192-bit security suite.
WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy): 64/128-bit, RC4, insecure/deprecated. WPA: TKIP. WPA2: CCMP/AES. WPA3: SAE. Enterprise mode uses RADIUS server (802.1X) for authentication.

Rogue AP: Fake access point to capture credentials. Evil Twin: AP impersonating a legitimate network. Deauthentication Attack: Forcing clients to disconnect (used in evil twin). Jamming: Disrupting wireless signals.

Infrastructure: Clients connect through an AP. Ad-hoc: Peer-to-peer without AP. Mesh: Devices relay for each other. Hotspot: Public wireless access. WDS: Wireless Distribution System for bridging APs.
Unicast: One-to-one. Multicast: One-to-many. Broadcast: One-to-all. Anycast: One-to-nearest. Geocast: Based on geographic location.
Maximum packet size that can be transmitted without fragmentation. Standard Ethernet MTU is 1500 bytes. Jumbo frames use 9000 bytes. Too large causes fragmentation; too small wastes bandwidth.

Type of Service (ToS) in IPv4 header, now Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP). QoS prioritizes traffic classes. EF (Expedited Forwarding) for voice, AF for assured forwarding, BE for best effort.
IEEE 802.1Q standard adds a 4-byte VLAN tag to Ethernet frames. Tag contains 12-bit VLAN ID (supports 4094 VLANs). Native VLAN (usually VLAN 1) carries untagged traffic.
Data VLAN: User traffic. Voice VLAN: VoIP traffic. Management VLAN: Switch management. Native VLAN: Untagged traffic on trunk. Default VLAN: VLAN 1 (should be changed).
Access port: Belongs to one VLAN, carries untagged traffic (connects to end devices). Trunk port: Carries traffic for multiple VLANs using 802.1Q tagging (connects switches to switches/routers).

Router-on-a-stick: Router with a single physical interface using sub-interfaces with 802.1Q. Layer 3 switch: Switch with routing capability. SVI (Switched Virtual Interface) provides Layer 3 gateway for VLANs.
Prevents Layer 2 loops by creating a tree topology. Elects Root Bridge (lowest Bridge ID). Blocking port prevents loops. Port states: Blocking, Listening, Learning, Forwarding, Disabled.
STP (802.1D): Original, slow convergence (30-50 sec). RSTP (802.1w): Rapid STP, faster convergence. MSTP (802.1s): Multiple Spanning Tree Protocol, maps VLANs to instances.
Propagates VLAN information across trunk links. Modes: Server (create/modify), Client (learn), Transparent (local only). VTP pruning reduces unnecessary broadcast traffic.
Detects unidirectional links where a device can transmit but not receive. Places port in error-disabled state. Prevents switching loops caused by broken fiber/cable.
